claims.text: Adding 2–4 at.% boron to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will improve its glass-forming ability.
Adding 2–4 at.% boron will increase the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous phase.
The boron intervention should remain effective under otherwise similar rapid-solidification and processing conditions.
Boron must remain a minor constituent for the proposed benefit to occur.
Severe pre-existing elemental segregation may limit the benefit of boron addition.
Boron will preferentially interact with phosphorus atoms.
Boron will preferentially interact with transition-metal atoms.
Boron-induced interactions will promote a more densely packed amorphous network.
Boron-induced interactions will promote a more chemically ordered amorphous network.
Enhanced chemical short-range order will disrupt crystal-nucleation pathways.
The boron-induced structural changes will reduce atomic rearrangements that lead to crystallization.
Reduced crystallization-related rearrangements will elevate the crystallization onset temperature.
The boron-modified alloy will require a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation than an otherwise identical boron-free alloy.
The boron-modified alloy will exhibit a higher crystallization onset temperature than an otherwise identical boron-free alloy.
Excessive boron may promote crystalline boride formation.
Crystalline boride formation or other effects at excessive boron levels may negate the proposed benefit.
The hypothesis is based on analogies with metallic-glass systems.
